and get back into bed.  He would then have had to pretend to be scared and
concerned when E.L. was discovered missing, and he would have had to call the
police on himself.  He would have had to run outside to where he had left E.L.
unattended for ten minutes, and deliver a number of very convincing screams
when he pretended to find her.

[
459
]

After
considering and weighing all of the evidence, including E.L.’s statements that
her father took her outside, the evidence regarding the state of the lock on
the front door, Sh.L.’s testimony that she heard footsteps going down the
stairs when S.L. was in the bedroom, the “whimpering” evidence, the testimony
of P.C. Thrush and the other evidence referred to above, I am satisfied beyond
a reasonable doubt that S.L. did not commit these offences.

Has the Crown established beyond a
reasonable doubt that R.G. did not commit

these offences?

[
460
]

I
am satisfied that there is no connection between R.G. and these offences other
than the fact that he was nearby when they took place and subsequently
witnessed certain events.  He heard a scream and a few minutes later saw a male
in the area.

[
461
]

R.G.
was excluded twice as the source of the male DNA found on E.L.’s pyjama top.
Both the cigarette butt he discarded outside 32 Division on January 3, 2012,
and the consent samples he provided to the police on October 21, 2013, were
analyzed.  The results were the same.  R.G.’s DNA was not located on E.L.’s
clothing.

[
462
]

The
defence submits that R.G. attempted to inject himself into the investigation.  According
to Det. Cst. Arruda, such behaviour can be a red flag: rather than running away
from the police, the perpetrator stays in contact with them in an effort to keep
tabs on any developments in the investigation.

[
463
]

Det.
Cst. Arruda viewed R.G. as
potentially
injecting himself into the
investigation on the basis that after he had given his statement to the police,
he continued to repeat his observations to other officers he encountered.
However, it is noteworthy that many of these encounters were instigated by the
police and not by R.G.  In my view, R.G.’s contacts with the police do not
support the conclusion that he was attempting to inject himself into this
investigation.

[
464
]

R.G.
approached P.C. Yim around 7:00 a.m. on December 26.  He asked P.C. Yim what
had happened.  P.C. Yim told him that there had been a major incident.  R.G.
stated that he had seen something that may or may not be important.  P.C. Yim,
who took a statement from R.G., described him as curious but co-operative and
helpful.  P.C. Yim later told Det. Cst. Landry about a witness who lived at 77
A. Street and who had seen someone running across his front yard.  P.C. Yim did
not mention R.G.’s name to Det. Cst. Landry.

[
465
]

Later
that morning, Det. Cst. Landry was taking photographs of houses on A. Street.
While he was photographing 77 A. Street, R.G. came out onto his porch and began
smoking a cigarette.  Det. Cst. Landry called out to him and asked him his
name.  R.G. obliged and identified himself.  Det. Cst. Landry did not observe
anything unusual about R.G.’s demeanour.  R.G. recounted the observations he
had made in the middle of the night, including the fact that the male who
jogged in front of his house had activated the motion detectors on the lights
at Numbers 79 and 81.  R.G. did not probe the officer for information regarding
the investigation.  In fact, Det. Cst. Landry did not recall R.G. asking him
any questions.

[
466
]

On
December 26, at 6:00 p.m., R.G. attended at 32 Division and provided a
DVD-recorded statement.  There is no suggestion that R.G. contacted the police
and asked if he could give a statement.  Presumably, the police requested him to
attend as a result of his statement to P.C. Yim.

[
467
]

On
December 27, at 2:00 a.m., R.G. was standing outside his residence at 77 A.
Street.  Inspector Narine decided to investigate him at that time.  R.G. told
him that he had provided a description of the suspect to the police and then
recounted his prior statement to P.C. Yim.

[
468
]

On
December 28, R.G. called Det. Cst. Akeson to advise him about the damage to the
fence separating his backyard from the backyard of D[…]2.  It was later learned
that P.C. Thrush caused this damage.

[
469
]

On
January 3, 2012, R.G. attended at 32 Division at the request of the police and
provided a consent sample of his DNA.

[
470
]

On
January 9 and 11, Det. Cst. Akeson initiated contact with R.G. in connection
with the composite sketch.  R.G.’s co-operation in this regard ultimately
resulted in a sketch, Exhibit 29, on January 12.

[
471
]

On
February 10, Det. Cst. Akeson contacted R.G. and requested him to take a
polygraph test.  R.G. initially agreed to take the test but then declined.  He testified
that he felt his word should be good enough.  He had already provided a consent
DNA sample.

[
472
]

R.G.
continued to co-operate with the police after Mr. Belbin’s arrest.  On February
20, 2012, he attended at 32 Division at the request of the police for the
purpose of viewing a photographic line-up.  On October 21, 2013, he provided a
second consent DNA sample.

[
473
]

It
is apparent that almost all of R.G.’s contacts with the police were initiated
by the police.  The only exceptions were his contact with P.C. Yim, to whom he
provided what he thought might be helpful information, and his call to Det.
Cst. Akeson to advise him about the damaged fence.  R.G. may have been curious
about what was going on.  He may, as the Crown suggested, have felt important
as a result of being involved as a witness in a major investigation.  However,
there is no suggestion that during his contact with the police he was trying to
keep tabs on the investigators or attempting to inject himself into their
investigation.

[
474
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that R.G. had a motive to commit a sexual assault on a
child.  Ms. Penman referred to the ten occurrences between 2003 and 2008 in
which R.G. was investigated by police in parking lots late at night.  On some
of these occasions, he was in possession of pornographic magazines.  Ms. Penman
submits that the motivation behind this behaviour was his fantasizing about
sexual activity with children and that on December 26, 2011, he acted out this
fantasy by abducting and sexually assaulting E.L.  R.G. adamantly denied having
any such fantasies or committing these offences.

[
475
]

In
my view, there is no basis to infer from these occurrences that R.G. had a
sexual interest in children.  First, although he was found in possession of
pornographic magazines, there is no suggestion that this material involved
children.  Otherwise, the police would have laid criminal charges. Secondly, R.G.
was found in the parking lots very late at night and not at a time when one
would expect to see children in the area.  For example, the times when the
police investigated him in the parking lot of the Phil White Arena ranged from
9:20 p.m. to 1:30 a.m.  He was found asleep in his vehicle at the Humewood
Community School at 4:00 a.m.  In 2006, the police came upon him in a parking
lot off Alberta Avenue at 1:00 a.m.  R.G. testified that no children were in
the area, at least not to his knowledge, on any of these occasions.  Finally, I
note that the last time R.G. was investigated was on April 24, 2008, over
three-and-a-half years prior to these offences.  On that date, he was issued a
ticket for loitering.  This appears to have had the appropriate deterrent
effect as there are no similar occurrences thereafter.  R.G. has no criminal
record.

[
476
]

The
parking lot incidents may be described as odd or peculiar, but there is no
common sense connection between them and E.L.’s abduction.

[
477
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that R.G.’s evidence about hearing a scream does not add
up – that it is improbable he could have heard S.L. screaming while watching a
show on his computer and using head phones.  I disagree.

[
478
]

R.G.
testified that the headphones sat lightly on his ears and the volume was not so
loud that it blocked out other sounds.  There were two windows in his apartment,
each of which was approximately 35 inches by 20 inches.  One of the windows was
open and had a fan running in it.  The fan may have blocked out some but not
necessarily all sounds coming from outside.  The other window faced the
backyard of D[…]2.  It was closed, but that does not mean that no sound could
have passed through it.  I also note that S.L.’s screams were very loud.  They
were so loud that they were picked up by the 911 tape as Sh.L. spoke to the
operator in the front hallway of D[…]1.  In all of the circumstances, I find R.G.’s
evidence that he heard a scream to be credible and reliable.  He testified that
the scream was the sound of someone in distress or being hurt, which is an
accurate description.

[
479
]

R.G.
also testified that at the same time that he heard the scream, he heard another
sound, which he admittedly had difficulty describing.  At trial, he described
it as a scuffle, as though someone was being dropped or pushed.  During his
police interview, he referred to it as a “shuffling, like when a person runs.”
He testified, however, that he did not believe he heard anyone running and
suggested that perhaps he had just been unable to adequately express to the
police what he had heard.  He still did not know how to describe the sound.  The
sound, whatever it was, in conjunction with the scream, left him with the
impression that there were “two guys fighting.”  That is why he waited a short
while before venturing outside to “have a peek” and smoke a cigarette.

[
480
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that R.G. made up the story about seeing a male emerge
from between two houses and jog past his house in order to divert the attention
of the police away from himself.  In support of this submission, Ms. Penman pointed
to several inconsistencies between R.G.’s testimony and his statement to police.
For example, R.G. testified that he noticed the flashlights in front of D[…]1
before

he observed the male.  He told the police that he saw the flashlights
after

he saw the male.  I do not place much weight on this discrepancy.  The timing
of his observation regarding the flashlights would likely not have seemed
terribly significant to R.G.

[
481
]

R.G.
testified that the male was wearing a hood that was tied up tightly under his
chin.  He agreed in cross-examination that he made no mention of this fact
during his police interview, although he did describe the toque as “tight to
the head.”  He denied the suggestion that this was a “new detail” that he has
added to his description of the male.  R.G.’s testimony that he has always
recalled that the hood was cinched tight is supported by the January 12 composite
sketch of the suspect created with his assistance.  In that sketch, the hood
appears to be drawn quite close to the suspect’s head.

[
482
]

During
his testimony, R.G. drew on a map the route that the male had taken.  His
drawing indicates that the male emerged from between 75 and 77 A. Street.  When
it was pointed out to him in cross-examination that he told the police that the
male had come out from between Numbers 73 and 75, R.G. more or less adopted his
previous statement and indicated that that was still his “main belief.”  He
went on to explain that he could not be exactly sure which two houses were
involved because the male was already about ten feet in front of the houses
when he first caught sight of him.  R.G.’s explanation makes some sense.
Again, I do not find this discrepancy particularly significant.  Both versions
involve the male emerging from between two houses that were east of R.G.’s
location.  He was standing at the northwest corner of his house and in the
shadows created by the street lighting at the time.

[
483
]

Although
R.G. was uncertain as to whether the male emerged from between Numbers 75 and
77, or Numbers 73 and 75, he has always maintained that the male disappeared
between Numbers 79 and 81.  The backyard of 81 A. Street is adjacent to the
backyard of D[…]3, where Mr. Belbin lived.  R.G. did not know Mr. Belbin.

[
484
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that an adverse inference should be drawn against R.G.
as a result of his refusal to take a polygraph test.  R.G. felt that his word
should be good enough.  Although his refusal is a factor for consideration, I
also take into account that up until that time, R.G. had co-operated fully with
the police: on December 26, he attended at 32 Division for a police interview;
on January 3, he re-attended to provide a consent sample of his DNA; and later
that month, he worked with a police artist in order to create the composite
sketch.

[
485
]

In
determining that R.G. was a person of interest, Det. Cst. Arruda observed some
similarities in the physical appearance of R.G. and S.L., which she felt might
be relevant in light of E.L.’s statements that her father was the person who
took her outside.  She thought that E.L. could have perhaps mistaken R.G. for
her father.

[
486
]

Det.
Cst. Arruda noted that both R.G. and S.L. had a beard and wore glasses.  They
both have brown hair and a somewhat similar build.  R.G. is 5 feet 4 inches
tall.  S.L. is 5 feet 6 ½ inches tall.  Other than these general similarities, however,
the two men do not look at all alike.  In addition, R.G., at age 52, is
substantially older than S.L., who is 31.

[
487
]

In
summary, I find that there is no basis upon which to conclude that R.G. had a
sexual interest in children and thus had a motive to commit these offences.  There
is also no basis on which to conclude that R.G. attempted to inject himself
into this investigation.  Other than his refusal to take a polygraph test, R.G.
co-operated with the police.  R.G. did not know the residents at D[…]1 and was
unaware that his landlady knew them until after the incident.

[
488
]

R.G.’s
DNA was not located on E.L.’s clothing.  If he were the perpetrator, he managed
to take E.L. from her bed, carry her downstairs, across the street and into the
backyard of D[…]2, place her on the ground and take off her clothes, including
her pyjama top, which was turned inside out in the process, without depositing his
DNA.

[
489
]

R.G.
was a night owl.  It was therefore not unusual for him to be awake at the time
when this incident took place.  I find that the circumstances were such that he
was in a position to hear S.L. screaming.  I accept his evidence that he went
outside a short time later and observed a male in a blue winter coat with a
hood.  I am satisfied that R.G.’s evidence with respect to the route taken by
that male is credible and reliable.  This route, which was described by R.G. to
the police on December 26, allows for the inference that the male was heading
in the direction of the accused’s residence.  R.G. did not know Mr. Belbin.
Nor was Mr. Belbin on the police radar at that time.  Mr. Belbin was not
canvassed by the police until December 28, and did not provide a sample of his
DNA until January 13, 2012.

[
490
]

After
considering all of the evidence and the submissions of counsel, I am satisfied
beyond a reasonable doubt that R.G. was not the perpetrator of these offences.

Has the Crown established beyond a
reasonable doubt that Ryan Belbin committed

these offences?

[
491
]

The
Crown’s position is that the only rational inference based on the evidence is
that Mr. Belbin committed these offences.  Ms. Cressman submits that the DNA
evidence alone, in the circumstances of this case, is sufficient to establish
Mr. Belbin’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.  She also submits that the
suspect’s flight path, as described by S.L., together with R.G.’s evidence
regarding the route taken by the male he observed shortly after the event,
point to Mr. Belbin as the perpetrator.  Ms. Cressman submits that the male
observed by R.G. was Mr. Belbin, who took this route in order to get back to
his home without being detected by the police.

[
492
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that the probability estimates provided by Mr. Currie
with respect to the DNA evidence cannot be relied on as none of the five
population groups appear to apply to the accused.  Ms. Penman further submits
that the DNA evidence is far from conclusive, given Mr. Currie’s testimony with
respect to the possibility of the indirect transfer of DNA from the ground to
the pyjama top and the potential for the transfer of DNA from one sleeve to the
other sleeve.   Ms. Penman takes the position that the DNA evidence alone
cannot support a conviction.  Furthermore, R.G.’s description of the male he
saw as white and clean shaven excludes Mr. Belbin as the perpetrator.  Ms.
Penman submits that when all the exculpatory evidence is taken into account,
including Mr. Belbin’s statements to police that he did not commit these
offences, there is more than a reasonable doubt as to his guilt.

The DNA evidence

[
493
]

The
DNA detected at two places on E.L.’s pyjama top – one on the left sleeve and
the other on the right sleeve – is the primary evidence against Mr. Belbin.

(i)
Potential for
contamination between the yarmulke, pyjama top, diaper and

pyjama
bottoms

[
494
]

There
was a potential for contamination or transfer of DNA between the pyjama top and
the other items of clothing seized from the backyard of D[…]2 as a result of
Det. Cst. Landry’s failure and Det. Cst. Arnott’s possible failure to re-glove
between handling each of those items.  I am satisfied that no such transfer
occurred.

[
495
]

Det.
Cst. Arnott collected the yarmulke, pyjama top, diaper and pyjama bottoms at
the scene.  He re-gloved before handling each item and placing it in its own
paper bag.  There was therefore no potential for DNA to be transferred from one
item to another at the scene.

[
496
]

Det.
Cst. Arnott also put on fresh gloves before he dealt with these items at the
Forensic Identification Unit later that day.  During his testimony, however, he
did not specifically mention re-gloving after handling each item.  Assuming
that he did not re-glove, there was the potential for a transfer of DNA from
one item to another at that time.

[
497
]

Det.
Cst. Arnott testified that he did not remove the yarmulke from its bag before
placing it on a shelf in the locker.  As a result, there was no opportunity for
DNA to be transferred from the yarmulke to the other items.   I note that in
light of Mr. Currie’s testimony with respect to the indirect transfer of DNA,
it would have been highly unlikely for Mr. Belbin’s DNA to have found its way
onto the yarmulke in any event.  The yarmulke belonged to S.L. and no doubt
blew off or fell off in the chaos at the scene and when he picked up E.L.
Assuming that it landed on the ground where pre-existing DNA from Mr. Belbin
was present, a transfer of his DNA to the yarmulke would not likely have
occurred unless pressure was applied (if the DNA sample was dry) or body heat
melted it (if the DNA sample was frozen).  Since neither of those factors was
at play, the issue of contamination from one item to another is limited to the
pyjama top, the diaper, and the pyjama bottoms.

[
498
]

Det.
Cst. Arnott removed those three items from their respective bags one at a time and
in that order, and hung each of them on individual hangers to dry.  The items
were not touching each other.

[
499
]

When
Det. Cst. Landry dealt with the items on December 28, 2011, he laid out fresh
paper on a table and put on fresh gloves.  He did not, however, change the
paper or re-glove before his examination of each item.

[
500
]

Det.
Cst. Landry first examined the yarmulke.  He found nothing unusual or
noteworthy about it and put it back into its bag.  He then examined the pyjama
top: it fluoresced under ASL lighting, indicating the presence of biological
matter.  Det. Cst. Landry then examined the diaper, followed by the pyjama
bottoms.  DNA from the pyjama top could theoretically have been transferred to the
diaper and the pyjama bottoms.  However, both items tested negative for the
presence of biological matter (i.e., they did not fluoresce under the ASL
lighting).  Therefore, such a transfer did not occur.

[
501
]

Thus,
although there was a potential for contamination between the yarmulke, pyjama
top, diaper and pyjama bottoms as a result of the failure to re-glove, the
evidence indicates that no such contamination actually took place.

(ii)
The DNA
Profiles on the pyjama top: Exhibits 13-3 and 13-5

[
502
]

The
entire pyjama top was subjected to testing for the presence of saliva and
semen.  A male DNA profile, which Mr. Currie referred to in his report as
Profile 2, was detected on two areas of the top (Exhibits 13-3 and 13-5).  Test
results were obtained at 15 loci on Exhibit 13-3 and at 11 loci on Exhibit 13-5.
Profile 2 “matched” Mr. Belbin’s DNA profile.

Exhibit 13-5

[
503
]

Exhibit
13-5 was taken from the front left sleeve.  It tested positive for amylase,
which is a protein that is present in high concentrations in saliva.  Testing
indicated the presence of a body fluid that contains amylase, but Mr. Currie
was unable to say whether that fluid was saliva, sweat, urine or feces.

[
504
]

Mr.
Belbin’s DNA profile matched Profile 2 detected on 13-5 at all 11 loci for
which there were test results.  Mr. Currie testified that there may be a number
of reasons why test results were obtained at only 11 locations on this exhibit.
He explained that when both a major and minor DNA profile are present, there
may be insufficient DNA to get results at all 15 loci.  I note that both E.L.’s
and Mr. Belbin’s DNA profile were present on Exhibit 13-5.  In addition, the
age of DNA can limit the test results as DNA degenerates over time.

Exhibit 13-3

[
505
]

The
test for the presence of semen involves testing for acid phosphatase, which is
present in very high levels in semen.  Acid phosphatase is also present in much
lower concentrations in sweat, urine, and feces, as well as in non-human
materials such as bacteria and fungus.

[
506
]

Exhibit
13-3, which was taken from the back lower right sleeve of the pyjama top,
tested positive for acid phosphatase.  However, based on the test result, Mr.
Currie could not say whether the source was from semen, sweat, urine, feces, or
a non-human material.  Mr. Currie opined that the acid phosphatase was
deposited on the pyjama top after it was laundered.   Amylase was not present
at this location.

[
507
]

There
were three DNA profiles detected on Exhibit 13-3:

i)

E.L.’s DNA profile;

ii)

Male
DNA Profile 2, which was developed at each of the 15 locations tested.  Mr.
Belbin’s DNA matched this profile at all 15 loci and thus he could not be
excluded as the source of this DNA; and

iii)

Profile
3, which was developed from Y-STR analysis.  S.L., A.L., another male relative,
M.L., and each of their paternal male relatives could not be excluded as the
source of Profile 3.

[
508
]

The
fact that Mr. Belbin cannot be excluded as the donor of Profile 2 on Exhibit
13-3 does not indicate whether the acid phosphatase detected in that area is
human or non-human.  Mr. Currie could not say one way or the other whether Mr.
Belbin’s DNA was related to or the source of the acid phosphatase.

[
509
]

Similarly,
the fact that S.L. cannot be excluded as the donor of Profile 3 on Exhibit 13-3
does not indicate whether the acid phosphatase is of human or non-human
origin.  It cannot be determined one way or the other as to whether S.L.’s DNA is
related to or the source of the acid phosphatase.

(iii)
Probability
analysis

[
510
]

Mr.
Currie based his probability analysis on data from a representative sample of
the Ontario population, which includes data from African Americans, Caucasians,
Asians, East Indians, and Northern Ontario Natives.  When he does not know a
suspect’s racial origin, as in this case, he calculates the estimated
probability for all five population groups, and then reports the most
conservative number.

[
511
]

For
Exhibit 13-3, the most conservative number was generated using data for the
East Indian population group.  This data indicates an estimated probability of
1 in 260 billion that a randomly selected individual, unrelated to Mr. Belbin, would
coincidentally share the DNA profile found on Exhibit 13-3.  For Caucasian and
African-American populations, the estimates were 1 in 420 billion and 1 in 1.1
trillion, respectively.

[
512
]

Mr.
Currie opined that the estimates provide very strong scientific support for the
hypothesis that Mr. Belbin is the source of male DNA Profile 2 found on the
right sleeve of the pyjama top.  He described the estimates as very
discriminating statistically.  [I note that the world population is only about
seven billion.]   Mr. Currie testified that the estimates would have been even
more discriminating if he had been able to assign specific frequency estimates
to all 15 loci, as opposed to just 13 loci.  However, the CFS does not currently
have population data for these two additional loci.

[
513
]

The
probability estimates were not as discriminating with respect to the DNA detected
on Exhibit 13-5, where there were test results at only 11 of 15 loci.  Mr.
Currie estimated a probability of 1 in 1.2 million that a randomly selected
individual, unrelated to Mr. Belbin, would coincidentally share the DNA profile
on Exhibit 13-5.  Again, he estimated this probability for all five population
groups and selected the most conservative number, in this case the Northern
Ontario Native data base.

[
514
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that the Court should place no weight on the probability
estimates, given that none of the five population groups appear to apply to Mr.
Belbin.  Ms. Penman noted that in his police interview on February 18, 2012,
Mr. Belbin stated that his mother was from Eastern Canada and currently lives
in Kingston, Ontario.  His father is from Trinidad but now lives in Cambridge,
Ontario.

[
515
]

In
my view, there is no evidentiary basis upon which to conclude that the
probability estimates are inapplicable to Mr. Belbin as a result of his mixed
racial background.  Such a proposition was never put to Mr. Currie during his
testimony.   What Mr. Currie did state was that when he does his probability
analysis, he does it “blind” or without knowing the racial origin of a suspect.
He calculates the probability estimates for each of the five population data
bases and then reports the most conservative number.  For Exhibit 13-3 the most
conservative number was 1 in 260 billion and was based on the East Indian
population group data.  Mr. Currie then referred to the probability estimates
for Caucasians and African Americans (which he refers to as Blacks in his
report), which are even more discriminating – 1 in 420 billion and 1 in 1.1
trillion, respectively.  Mr. Currie concluded that the probability estimates in
this case provide strong scientific support for the hypothesis that Mr. Belbin
is the source of DNA Profile 2 on the back lower right sleeve of the pyjama
top.  He opined that it would be an extremely unlikely coincidence that someone
other than Mr. Belbin was the source of that DNA.

[
516
]

As
I understand Mr. Currie’s testimony, the population data bases used by the CFS are
intended to reflect the
Ontario population

as a whole
.  That
population is extremely diverse and includes many people with mixed racial
backgrounds.  At no point in his testimony did Mr. Currie state that the probability
estimates are inapplicable to persons of mixed racial heritage.  Rather, he
testified that when a suspect’s racial origin is unknown to him, which is
usually the case when he does his calculations, the appropriate approach is to
rely on the most conservative probability estimate generated from the five
population data bases, which is what he did in this case.

[
517
]

Considering
that the most conservative probability estimate is 1 in 260 billion, along with
the fact that Mr. Belbin lived only two doors down from where the pyjama top
was found, the prospect of anyone other than Mr. Belbin being the donor of DNA
Profile 2 on the back lower right sleeve (Exhibit 13-3) of the pyjama top is almost
negligible.  The probability estimate with respect to the DNA on the front left
sleeve (Exhibit 13-5) is not as discriminating but is still significant when
considered along with the findings relating to Exhibit 13-3.

[
518
]

I
am satisfied that Mr. Belbin was the source of Profile 2 on both the right and
left sleeve of the pyjama top.

(iv)
The
transfer of DNA – direct and indirect

[
519
]

The
question of
how
Mr. Belbin’s DNA ended up on E.L.’s pyjama top – whether
it was by direct or indirect transfer – is a live issue in this case.  However,
the question of
when
Mr. Belbin’s DNA was transferred to the top is
clear.  Based on the evidence, the transfer had to have occurred at some point between
the time that E.L. was taken from her bed and the time that the perpetrator fled
the scene.

[
520
]

In
determining this timeframe, I have taken into account that the pyjamas were freshly
laundered in Connecticut and had not been worn by E.L. prior to the evening of
December 25.  S.L. put them on her after her bath and just before she went to
bed.  The pyjamas were not exposed to the outdoors during her visit here.  It
is also relevant that Mr. Belbin was a stranger to the L. family.  He was
neither a friend nor an acquaintance of any of the residents at D[…]1 and he had
never been in their house.  Mr. Belbin himself, in his statement to Det.
Thomas, denied knowing the family.   It is clear from these circumstances that
Mr. Belbin’s DNA was not on E.L.’s pyjama top prior to her being abducted from
her bed.

[
521
]

There
was a period of approximately 15 minutes during which time the pyjama top was
left unguarded in the backyard of D[…]2; that is, from the time that the
perpetrator fled the scene to the time that the police arrived.  S.L.
discovered E.L. and her assailant about four minutes after he called 911 at
3:23 a.m.  At 3:40 a.m., Sgt. Cowan and P.C. Thrush arrived.  Neither of them touched
the pyjamas.  There was no one in the backyard at that time.  Sgt. Cowan
remained on the west side of the property to ensure that no one entered the
yard.  Commencing at 3:52 a.m., the clothes were guarded by a series of
officers until Det. Cst. Arnott seized them later that morning.

[
522
]

There
is no evidence to suggest that Mr. Belbin’s DNA was deposited on the pyjama top
during the 15 minutes that it was left unguarded.  In fact, Mr. Belbin was
clear in his statements to the police that he was home at that time.  He told
Detectives Christie and Luff, who questioned him during a canvas of the
neighbourhood on December 28, that he was in his apartment on December 26
between midnight and 6:00 a.m.  On January 13, 2012, he told Det. Cst.
Villaflor that he went to bed at 10:30 p.m. on December 25 and did not wake up
until 9:30 a.m. on December 26.  He also stated that he had remained in his
apartment from Friday, December 23, until Tuesday, December 27, when he
returned to work.  On February 18, 2012, Mr. Belbin told Det. Thomas that he
remained in his residence for five days straight.  Other than shopping at the
No Frills store on December 23, he stayed inside from that day onward until
Wednesday, December 28, when he went to work.

[
523
]

Mr.
Belbin’s statements rule out any possibility that his DNA was deposited on E.L.’s
pyjama top between the time that the perpetrator fled and the arrival of the
police about 15 minutes later.

[
524
]

Direct
or indirect transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA to the pyjama top could only have
occurred from the time that E.L. was taken from her bed, which was probably
around 3:20 a.m., to when S.L. found her in the backyard and the perpetrator
took off.  By the time the first police officers arrived on scene, which was
3:28 a.m., S.L. had already returned to the house with E.L.  The interval of
time during which Mr. Belbin’s DNA was transferred to the pyjamas is therefore
quite brief.

[
525
]

Mr.
Currie testified that direct transfer occurs when a person leaves their DNA on
an item by touching it or expels DNA onto the item through actions such as
coughing, sneezing, or ejaculation.  According to Mr. Currie’s testimony, Mr.
Belbin’s touching of Esther’s pyjama top in the course of removing it would be
sufficient to transfer his DNA onto the top.  Mr. Currie could not say whether Mr.
Belbin’s DNA on the right sleeve was semen, sweat, urine, or feces.  He was
also unable to identify the body fluid that was the source of Mr. Belbin’s DNA
on the left sleeve.  It could be saliva, sweat, urine or feces.

[
526
]

Mr.
Currie testified that an indirect transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA onto the pyjama
top would be possible in certain circumstances, assuming that Mr. Belbin happened
to have spat or urinated on the same spot where the pyjama top made contact
with the ground.  However, barring factors that may have assisted in preserving
the DNA, such as a cold dry environment, Mr. Belbin’s DNA would have had to
have been left on the ground recently.  Mr. Currie explained that DNA begins to
degrade once it has left the body and is exposed to moisture, bacteria, heat or
sunlight.  Contact with soil hastens the degradation process.  Age itself is a
factor.  Mr. Currie testified that he did not detect any signs of degradation
when assessing DNA Profile 2.

[
527
]

Based
on Mr. Belbin’s statement to Det. Thomas as to his whereabouts around the time
of the offence, the latest date on which Mr. Belbin could have spat or urinated
in the backyard of D[…]2 would have been Friday, December 23.  Mr. Belbin told Det.
Thomas that other than his trip to No Frills on that day, he remained in his
apartment from Friday to Wednesday morning.  Assuming that Mr. Belbin spat or urinated
in the backyard of D[…]2 on Friday afternoon, his DNA would have been exposed
to the environment for about 2 ½ days by the time E.L. was carried into the yard
and placed on the ground where his DNA happened to be located.

[
528
]

Mr.
Currie was asked whether DNA could be transferred to a child’s pyjamas in the
following scenario: a person spits or urinates on a spot on the ground in cold
weather.  A couple of days later, a child wearing pyjamas is put on the same
spot on the ground.  A certain amount of force or pressure is applied to her
and her pyjamas are removed.  Mr. Currie testified that there is a possibility
that the DNA could be transferred to the pyjamas if the DNA is relatively fresh
in terms of moisture.  If the saliva or urine has dried over time, then just
placing the garment on top of it would probably not result in a transfer.  He
explained that dry contact is not a very efficient means of transferring DNA
from one object to another.  Pressure between the DNA sample and the garment
would be required to enable the transfer to occur or, in the alternative,
something that caused rehydration of the DNA cells; for example, if the pyjama
top were moist, it could rehydrate the cells.  The cells could also be
rehydrated by rain or melted snow.

[
529
]

Mr.
Currie testified that DNA could be transferred if the saliva or urine froze so
quickly that there was no opportunity for the DNA to degrade, and the saliva or
urine was then returned to a liquid state by reason of the child’s body heat or
a warmer outside temperature.

[
530
]

Crown
counsel submits that the fact that Mr. Belbin’s DNA is on both sleeves reduces the
likelihood that it got there via an indirect transfer from the ground since the
same phenomenon that allowed for such a transfer would have had to occur independently
at both Exhibits 13-3 and 13-5.  Ms. Cressman submits that this would be a highly
unlikely scenario.  Each sleeve would just happen to have touched a spot on the
ground where Mr. Belbin’s DNA was present.  If frozen, the DNA sample on each spot
on the ground would then have to have been warmed in some way in order to
facilitate a transfer to each sleeve.  If the DNA samples were dry, pressure
between each of the DNA samples and the sleeves would have to be applied in
order for a transfer to occur.

[
531
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that an indirect transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA onto the
pyjama top need only have occurred on one sleeve and that the DNA from that
sleeve could then have been transferred to the other sleeve later on.  She
based this submission on Mr. Currie’s testimony as to how indirect transfers generally
occur.  Mr. Currie was never asked directly as to whether the evidence supports
or undermines the proposition that Mr. Belbin’s DNA was transferred from
Exhibit 13-3 to Exhibit 13-5, or vice versa.

[
532
]

There
are a number of factors regarding the analyses of Exhibits 13-3 and 13-5 which
raise questions in the Court’s mind as to whether such a transfer took place.
These concerns arise mainly as a result of the differences between the two
exhibits.  For example, 13-5 tested positive for amylase but 13-3 contained no
amylase.  If there was a transfer of DNA from 13-3 to 13-5 or vice-versa, why
would amylase not be present in both areas?  Similar reasoning could also be
applied with respect to the presence of acid phosphatase, which was detected in
13-3 but not in 13-5.  Another difference is the fact that there were three DNA
profiles on 13-3 and only two DNA profiles on 13-5.

[
533
]

Unfortunately,
Mr. Currie was never questioned with respect to the significance, if any, of
these differences.  They may be important or they may have no bearing whatsoever
on the issue of whether Mr. Belbin’s DNA was transferred from one sleeve to the
other.  In the absence of expert testimony in this regard, I will assume that
there was the potential for a transfer of DNA between Exhibits 13-3 and 13-5.

[
534
]

Mr.
Currie’s testimony allows for the possibility that a person’s DNA from spit or
urine on the ground could, in certain circumstances, be transferred to an
article of clothing with which it comes into contact.  Whether the transfer
takes place depends on many factors, including the age of the DNA and its
freshness in terms of moisture.  There are a whole host of factors that cannot
be controlled for and that play a role in the degradation of DNA, such as
sunlight, moisture, bacteria, and contact with the soil.  If Mr. Belbin’s DNA
were on the ground in the backyard of D[…]2, it would have been exposed to all
of these factors for a minimum of 2 or 2 ½ days, assuming that he spat or
urinated in the yard on December 23.  Mr. Currie did not detect any signs of
degradation when assessing DNA Profile 2.

[
535
]

In
summary, based on Mr. Currie’s testimony, I make the following findings:

1.

Although
there was a potential for contamination between the yarmulke, pyjama top,
diaper, and pyjama bottoms as a result of the failure of Det. Cst. Landry and
possible failure of Det. Cst. Arnott to re-glove, no such contamination
actually took place.

2.

The
probability estimates provided by Mr. Currie, coupled with the fact that Mr.
Belbin lived only a few doors down from where this incident took place,
establish that Mr. Belbin was the source of DNA Profile 2 that was detected on
the right and left sleeve of the pyjama top.

3.

In
the absence of expert testimony to the contrary, I will presume that there was
a potential for a transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA from Exhibit 13-3 to Exhibit
13-5, or vice versa, as submitted by counsel for Mr. Belbin.

4.

Direct
or indirect transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA to the pyjama top could only have
occurred between the time that E.L. was taken from her bed and the time that S.L.
found her, at which point the perpetrator fled.

5.

If
Mr. Belbin touched E.L.’s pyjama top in the course of removing it, such
touching would be sufficient to transfer his DNA onto the top.

6.

There
is the possibility that Mr. Belbin’s DNA from spit or urine on the ground
could, in certain circumstances, be transferred to an article of clothing that
came into contact with it. A number of factors would have to align in a certain
way before such a transfer took place.

[
536
]

With
respect to No. 6 above, a transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA from the ground to the
pyjama top would be impossible if Mr. Belbin’s DNA from spit or urine was not
on the ground in the first place.  For the reasons given later on in this
judgment, I find that there is no evidentiary basis upon which to infer that
Mr. Belbin deposited his DNA in the backyard of D[…]2 by spitting or urinating
there.

The perpetrator’s direction of flight

[
537
]

As
previously stated, S.L.’s opportunity to observe the suspect was extremely
limited.  He only saw him for five or six seconds, never saw his face, only saw
his back, and the lighting was less than ideal.  The suspect was hunched over E.L.
but he immediately got up and ran away when S.L. appeared on the scene.  S.L.
was in a state of emotional turmoil at the time.  It is understandable that in
these circumstances he was unable to provide a detailed description of the
suspect and why he may have been confused about such things as the colour of
the suspect’s clothing.  He told the 911 operator that the suspect was wearing
sweatpants, a sweatshirt and maybe a hood.  He testified that he was pretty
sure that the sweatshirt was dark but, as I have already reviewed in these
reasons, he told the first officers on the scene that it was white.  He thought
that the suspect was his height or a little taller, although he told P.C.
Leonard and P.C. Vandercamp, respectively, that the suspect was 5 feet 6 inches
and 5 feet 5 inches to 5 feet 6 inches.  He had an average build and was not “too
huge”.

[
538
]

Given
the circumstances in which S.L. made his observations, not too much weight can
be placed on his description of the suspect.  However, I find his testimony reliable
with respect to the suspect’s direction of flight – that he ran east and
struggled to get over something on the eastern portion of the property line.

[
539
]

When
S.L. went down the west side of D[…]2 in search of E.L., he ended up at the northwest
corner of the house.  He found himself looking at the suspect’s back.  He
screamed.  The suspect got up and took off.  It makes sense that the suspect would
run east or straight ahead and away from the person who was screaming.  S.L.’s
description of the suspect struggling with something, as though he were
climbing over something, is consistent with the suspect trying to get over the
railing on the east side of the deck, which runs along the back of the house.

[
540
]

The
fact that the suspect fled in an easterly direction is significant as it allows
for the inference that the suspect was the same person that R.G. saw a short
time later.  R.G. heard a scream, waited a minute or so, and then went out to look
around and smoke a cigarette.  He was standing at the northwest corner of his
house at 77 A. Street when he saw a male coming from the east.  He did not
actually see the male emerge from between two houses and, as a result, was not
sure whether he came from between Numbers 75 and 77 or Numbers 73 and 75 A.
Street.  He thought it was probably the latter two houses.  In either case, the
suspect, in order to get to those properties, would simply have had to run east
through the backyard of D[…]2, as described by S.L., and cut into the backyards
of Numbers 73, 75, or 77 A. Street.

[
541
]

The
suspect would no doubt have avoided D[…] as the police were on scene very
quickly.  Two officers had arrived at D[…]1 by the time the 911 call ended.  R.G.
recalled seeing flashlights in front of D[…]1 while he was outside.

[
542
]

Given
the police presence, Mr. Belbin, if he were the suspect, could not have walked
back to his house along D[…] without being detected.  However, he could have reached
his house and avoided the police by running between either Numbers 73 and 75,
or 75 and 77 A. Street and out to the curb, jogging past 77 A. Street, and cutting
back between the properties at Numbers 79 and 81 A. Street, as described by R.G.
The path between Numbers 79 and 81 is quite wide.  There is no gate blocking
access to the backyard of 81 A. Street, which adjoins the backyard of D[…]3,
where Mr. Belbin lived.  The backyards of 81 A. Street and D[…]3 are separated
by a chain link fence that would not be difficult to scale.

[
543
]

As
stated earlier, at the time that R.G. told Officers Yim and Landry about his
observations, Mr. Belbin was not on the police radar with respect to this
investigation.  He was not even identified as a person of interest until a
couple of days later.  R.G. did not know Mr. Belbin or where he lived.  There
was no reason for R.G. to fabricate his evidence about having seen a male take
the route that he described in the early hours of the morning on December 26.

[
544
]

R.G.
described the male as about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 180
pounds.  He had a good build – “healthy” and “strong.”  These descriptors are
consistent with Mr. Belbin’s appearance.  R.G. thought the male was about 19
years old.  Mr. Belbin was 28 years old at the time of this incident but is
quite youthful in appearance, as is evident from the photograph taken of him on
the day of his arrest and which was included in the photographic line-up shown
to R.G. on February 20, 2012.

[
545
]

R.G.
did not see the male’s hair as he was wearing a winter coat with a hood, which was
tied up tightly under his chin.  The male also wore a toque, a small portion of
which was visible where it came down onto his forehead from under the hood.

[
546
]

R.G.
testified that there was nothing distinctive about the winter coat, which was
blue in colour.  He described it as plain.  There was no pattern or writing on
it.

[
547
]

When
asked about the man’s skin colour, R.G. stated that he “seemed like a Caucasian,
a white.” He was clean shaven.  His face was “youngish” and smooth.

[
548
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that R.G.’s description of the male as white and clean
shaven is exculpatory evidence:  it excludes Mr. Belbin as the perpetrator because
Mr. Belbin has a mixed racial background (although I note that his complexion
is fairly light) and he is not clean shaven.  As stated by the court in
Chartier
v. Quebec (Attorney General)
, [1979] S.C.R. 474 at p. 19, if there is one
dissimilar characteristic between a witness’s description and a suspect, there
is no identification regardless of the number of similar characteristics.

[
549
]

Ms.
Penman submits that R.G.’s description of the man’s skin tone and facial hair
should be accepted as reliable in light of R.G.’s own assertion that “he got a
pretty good look at the person” and the fact that R.G. was not in an emotional
state when he made his observations.  There was also street lighting in the
area.

[
550
]

I
do not view the “clean shaven” descriptor as a characteristic that necessarily excludes
Mr. Belbin since there is no evidence to indicate whether or not he was clean
shaven on December 26, 2011.  The only evidence before the court in terms of
Mr. Belbin’s facial hair are his DVD-recorded police interviews on January 13
and February 18, 2012, and his photograph taken on February 18, which was used
in the photographic line-up.  On both January 13 and February 18, Mr. Belbin
had some light facial hair that was akin to or somewhat heavier than a five-o’clock
shadow.

[
551
]

Although
R.G. stated that he got a good look at the male, the evidence indicates that
his opportunity to observe his facial features was, in fact, very limited.  The
male jogged around R.G. in what was basically a semi-circle.  The closest that
he came to him was 20 to 25 feet, which was when he was jogging past his house.
R.G. had less than a minute, perhaps only thirty seconds, in which to observe
him.  For at least part of that time, R.G. would probably only have seen the
man’s profile.  The male never looked in his direction.  Although there was some
street lighting, it was not the equivalent of making the same observations in
daylight.

[
552
]

R.G.
may have been confident about his ability to identify the man but the fact that
a witness is confident does not necessarily bear on his or her actual ability
to make an identification.  Given the very limited time in which he could view the
male, the distances between himself and that person (the closest distance being
20 to 25 feet for what would have been only a few seconds), and the time of day
when he made his observations, R.G. was far from being in a good position to observe
the man’s facial features or his skin tone.  In the circumstances, I do not
view R.G.’s description of the male as white and clean shaven as sufficiently
reliable such that either descriptor can or should be regarded as a “dissimilar
feature” in terms of the identification of Mr. Belbin.

[
553
]

It
was not until almost three weeks after this incident that R.G. worked with a
police artist to produce a composite sketch of the male.  The eyes of the male
depicted in that sketch are closed or looking down.  The male does not look
like Mr. Belbin but has a rather generic appearance, which is not surprising
given R.G.’s limited opportunity to observe the male’s facial features.  Two
months after the incident, R.G. failed to identify Mr. Belbin from a
photographic line-up, which again is hardly surprising, given the passage of
time and R.G.’s limited opportunity for observation of the man’s face.

[
554
]

Although
R.G.’s observations of the male’s facial features and skin tone cannot be
regarded as reliable, his description of the route taken by the male is highly
reliable.  R.G. reported that route to Officers Yim and Landry only a few hours
after the event, when it was still fresh in his mind.  His description of the
male’s approximate age, size, stature, and the way he was moving, may also be regarded
as reliable and are consistent with Mr. Belbin’s appearance.

The blue winter jacket

[
555
]

R.G.
described the male as wearing a plain blue winter coat with a hood.  He stated
that there was nothing distinctive about it.  A blue jacket with a hood was
found in Mr. Belbin’s apartment during the execution of a search warrant.

[
556
]

There
is no forensic evidence linking Mr. Belbin’s jacket to the crime scene.  The
jacket was never submitted to the CFS for DNA analysis since ASL testing for the
presence of biological substances proved negative.  The fabric and exact colour
of the jacket are unknown as neither the jacket nor any photographs of it were tendered
as exhibits.  The jacket was not shown to R.G. or S.L. for identification
purposes.  In these circumstances, little weight can be attributed to the “blue
jacket” evidence.

The application of W.(D.)

[
557
]

The
principles in
W.(D.)

apply in this case.  If I believe Mr. Belbin’s
statements to the police that he did not commit these offences, then I must
find him not guilty.  Even if I do not believe Mr. Belbin’s statements of
denial, I must acquit Mr. Belbin if I have a reasonable doubt as a result of those
statements and other evidence favourable to the defence.  Finally, even if that
evidence does not leave me with a reasonable doubt, I must still go on to
determine whether the Crown has proved Mr. Belbin’s guilt beyond a reasonable
doubt.  In assessing Mr. Belbin’s statements, I am entitled to consider them in
the context of all of the other evidence.

[
558
]

The
evidence favourable to the defence includes E.L.’s statements that her father
took her outside, and the other evidence relied on by the defence in support of
its position that the Crown has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that
S.L. did not commit these offences.  However, for the reasons already stated, I
found that little weight can be attributed to E.L.’s statements.  I have also
found that when all of the evidence is considered as a whole, the Crown has
established beyond a reasonable doubt that S.L. did not abduct and sexually
assault his daughter.

[
559
]

Similarly,
the evidence relied on by the defence in support of its position that R.G. was
the perpetrator is potentially exculpatory.  However, for the reasons already
stated, after considering all of the evidence, I am satisfied beyond a
reasonable doubt that R.G. did not commit these offences.

[
560
]

I
have also found that R.G.’s description of the male he observed that night as
“white” and “clean shaven” is not reliable, given R.G.’s very limited
opportunity to observe the male’s skin tone and facial features.  As a result,
neither of those descriptors can be regarded as a “dissimilar feature” in terms
of the identification of Mr. Belbin.

[
561
]

In
addition, I have found that the dissimilarity between Mr. Belbin and the
composite sketch, and R.G.’s failure to identify Mr. Belbin from a photographic
line-up on February 20, are of little evidentiary value, again as the result of
R.G.’s very limited opportunity to see the man’s face, as well as the passage
of time.  The composite sketch was not created until January 12.  The
photographic line-up was not conducted until February 20, some two months after
the event.

[
562
]

The
statements made by Mr. Belbin to the police on December 28, January 13, and
February 18, were not given under oath.  There was no opportunity for
cross-examination, although Det. Thomas was quite persistent in his questioning.

[
563
]

On
December 28, Detectives Christie and Luff spoke only briefly to Mr. Belbin in
the hallway outside his apartment.  The conversation lasted three to five
minutes.  Mr. Belbin told the officers that he was home on December 26 between
midnight and 6:00 a.m. and that he did not see or hear anything unusual during
that period.

[
564
]

Det.
Cst. Villaflor’s interview of Mr. Belbin at police headquarters on January 13
lasted about 15 minutes.  One of the first questions Det. Cst. Villaflor asked
him, after making a few introductory remarks, was whether he took “that girl
out of her home.”  Mr. Belbin answered, “No.”  Det. Cst. Villaflor then asked
him what he was doing on the night of December 25 and the early hours of
December 26.  Mr. Belbin replied that he went to bed on December 25 at about
10:30 p.m. and woke up the next morning at 9:30 a.m.  He had gone shopping on
Thursday, December 22.  He did not leave his apartment from Friday until
Monday.  He returned to work on Tuesday.  He did not have a view of D[…] from
his apartment.

[
565
]

Det.
Cst. Villaflor asked Mr. Belbin for a sample of his DNA, which Mr. Belbin
provided after the consent form was read and explained to him.  Det. Cst.
Villaflor had not told Mr. Belbin prior to his arrival at the police station
that he would be requesting a DNA sample.  The fact that Mr. Belbin provided
the sample is after-the-fact conduct capable of supporting an inference
favourable to the accused.

[
566
]

During
Det. Thomas’ interview of Mr. Belbin on February 18, Mr. Belbin responded to
questions about his family history and background.  He also asserted on a
number of occasions that he was innocent of these offences.  He stated that he
was being accused because of where he lived, that he had “nothing to do with it,”
and that he was telling the truth when he denied taking “that little girl” out
of the house.  He stated that it was not possible that his DNA matched the DNA detected
at the crime scene and that he thought Det. Thomas was lying to him about his
DNA being on the complainant’s clothing.

[
567
]

Crown
counsel took the position during her submissions that if there were some
scenario or innocent explanation for Mr. Belbin’s DNA to be present in the
backyard of D[…]2, he had ample opportunity to tell Det. Thomas about it.
However, I draw no adverse inference in this regard as it presumes that Mr.
Belbin was knowledgeable about DNA and the ways in which it may be transferred
to an object.

[
568
]

Mr.
Belbin told Det. Thomas that he was in his apartment from the time he got home
from work on Thursday, December 22, until Tuesday and that he returned to work
on Wednesday, December 28.  The only time he left the apartment was on Friday,
when he walked to the No Frills store at Bathurst and Wilson to shop for
groceries.  When Det. Thomas suggested that five days was a long time to remain
in an apartment, Mr. Belbin replied that he realized that, but he had “so many
things to do in the apartment.”  It was winter.  He slept a lot.  He was also
sorting through shows he had recorded on a satellite service.

[
569
]

Defence
counsel submits that the proposition that Mr. Belbin spent his entire vacation inside
his apartment is reasonable or at least not surprising in light of the fact
that he had very few friends and was not close to his mother.  Mr. Belbin did
not have a view of D[…] from his apartment and did not know the family that
lived at D[…]1.  Ms. Penman submits that in these circumstances, Mr. Belbin could
not have known that there were children visiting at that address.  S.L. and his
family did not arrive at his parents’ home until about 11:00 p.m. on December
22.   The children were asleep and were carried into the house.

[
570
]

In
my view, Mr. Belbin’s assertion that he remained in his basement apartment from
Thursday after work until he returned to work on Wednesday morning, with the
exception of his trip to No Frills on Friday, is problematic, even allowing for
the fact that he had few friends or close relatives with whom he might have visited
or socialized.  Five days is a substantial and unusually long period of time to
remain within the confines of one’s home.  I note that Mr. Belbin told Det.
Cst. Villaflor that he had gone shopping on Thursday, as opposed to Friday, and
had returned to work on Tuesday, as opposed to Wednesday.

[
571
]

Had
Mr. Belbin been outside his apartment on more occasions than he was willing to admit
to Det. Cst. Villaflor or Det. Thomas, he would have had the opportunity to
observe the comings and goings of the L. family members as they ran errands and
went to and from various social events, starting on Friday morning and
continuing over the course of the weekend.  It is clear that at the very least,
based on Mr. Belbin’s statement to Det. Thomas, that he may have had that
opportunity on Friday, when he left his apartment to go to No Frills and when
he returned home.  Mr. Belbin would most likely have walked right past D[…]1 on
his way to the store, which was at the corner of Bathurst and Wilson.

[
572
]

The
evidence indicates that E.L. and T.L. were in and out of the house on a couple
of occasions on Friday.  H.L. drove them to a plaza sometime after 9:30 a.m.
They returned home around 11:00 a.m.   In the early afternoon, S.L. drove H.L.
and the two girls to the same No Frills store that Mr. Belbin attended.  They
returned home after stopping at a couple of other shops.

[
573
]

I
note that Mr. Belbin was somewhat evasive when Det. Thomas questioned him about
the timing of his excursion to No Frills on Friday.  He told Det. Thomas that
he could not remember when he left his apartment to go to the store or when he
returned home.  He could not even recall the time of day that he was at the
store.  He stated: “Could’ve been any time.  I used to go there early but I
haven’t most recently – whenever – whenever I can – whenever I can get there
when I’m not busy.”

[
574
]

The
fact that Mr. Belbin walked to the store and walked home meant that there were
two different occasions on which he may have observed E.L. entering or leaving D[…]1.

[
575
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin submits that since Mr. Belbin had never been in D[…]1 and did
not know the people who lived there, he would not have known where the children
were sleeping.  However, the layout of the house was such that the children’s
bedroom could be seen from the front entrance hall.  A stranger entering the
house would be able to see right up the stairs and into the room.  The girls’
twin beds could not be seen from that location but a crib in the south east
corner of the room was visible.  The children’s bedroom door had been left wide
open.  There was a lamp in the room that was usually turned down low.  Based on
the evidence of the L. family members, I find that the ceiling light in the
upstairs hallway outside the three bedrooms was on, as was the light in the
bathroom off that hallway.  The doors to the other two bedrooms were closed,
although Sh.L. and S.L. had left their door somewhat ajar.  Given the layout of
the house and the lighting, the location of the children’s bedroom would have
been obvious to a stranger entering the home through the front door in the
middle of the night.

[
576
]

In
summary, I did not find Mr. Belbin’s unsworn statements to the police that he
did not commit these offences to be credible or reliable.  In reaching this
conclusion, I have considered the statements in the context of all of the
evidence.  His statements of denial, the fact that he provided a sample of his
DNA to the police, and the other evidence favourable to the defence, do not
leave me with a reasonable doubt when considered in the context of all of the
evidence.  In accordance with the
W. (D.)
analysis, I must go on to
determine whether the Crown has proved its case on the basis of the evidence
that I do accept.

The Crown’s case

[
577
]

There
can be no doubt, based on the probability estimates provided by Mr. Currie, coupled
with the fact that Mr. Belbin lived only a few doors down from where this
incident took place, that he was the source of DNA Profile 2 found on the right
and left sleeve of E.L.’s pyjama top.

[
578
]

There
can be no doubt that Mr. Belbin’s DNA was transferred to the pyjama top at some
point between the time that E.L. was abducted from her bed and the time that
the perpetrator fled the backyard of D[…]2.

[
579
]

There
is no doubt that E.L.’s assailant removed her pyjama top and tossed it aside, leaving
it inside out.   Based on Mr. Currie’s testimony, if Mr. Belbin touched the
pyjama top in the course of removing it, such touching would be sufficient to
transfer his DNA onto the top.

[
580
]

Mr.
Currie also allowed for the possibility that Mr. Belbin’s DNA from spit or
urine on the ground could, in certain circumstances, be transferred to an
article of clothing that came into contact with it.  A number of factors would
have to align in a certain way before such a transfer took place.  However, such
a transfer would be impossible if Mr. Belbin’s DNA were not on the ground in
the first place.

[
581
]

I
find that there is no evidentiary basis upon which to infer that Mr. Belbin
deposited his DNA in the backyard of D[…]2 by spitting or urinating there.
Such a proposition is based on mere speculation or conjecture.

[
582
]

According
to his statement to Det. Thomas, Mr. Belbin did not have many friends and had
no friends in the neighbourhood.  He had some acquaintances by virtue of his
job delivering newspapers twice a week, a job that he held until the second
week in December.  Mr. Belbin explained to Det. Thomas that by “acquaintances”
he meant people to whom he would say “Hi” or with whom he would have a quick
conversation if he happened to see them.  People who wanted their paper would
sometimes be waiting at their door, in which case they would greet him.

[
583
]

As
Mr. Belbin did not know and was not friends with the residents at D[…]2, there
was no logical reason for him to trespass into their backyard.  It is unlikely
and does not make any sense that he would urinate there, given the fact that
his own residence was only two houses down the street.  The area of the
backyard where E.L.’s pyjamas were found was some distance from the front door
and would have had nothing to do with the delivery of newspapers to that
address.  There is no scenario to account for Mr. Belbin’s DNA being in the
backyard by reason of his delivering newspapers.

[
584
]

The
reasoning in
R. v. McLeod
,
2010 SKCA 43
, leave to appeal to SCC refused,
2010 CanLll 41566, which admittedly deals with an aspect of DNA evidence other
than the issue of transfer, is nevertheless applicable in this case.

[
585
]

In

McLeod
, the appellant was convicted of first degree murder solely on the
basis of DNA evidence.  On appeal, he argued that the trial judge erred in
failing to take proper account of the impact of “related populations” on random
match probabilities.  It was argued that if a blood relative (such as a
brother), was a possible source of the DNA detected on items found at the crime
scene, the random match probabilities generated by the expert witnesses would
require adjustment.

[
586
]

In
dismissing the appeal, the Court observed, at para. 30, that there was no
evidence to suggest that the appellant had a brother, or any other blood
relative for that matter and, more specifically, no evidence to suggest a
brother or a blood relative might be a suspect in the murder of the victim.
The court relied on the reasoning in
R. v. Adams
,
[1996] 2 Cr. App. R.
467 (C.A.)
, which was a rape case in which the only evidence against the
accused was the DNA evidence.  At p. 470, the Court of Appeal stated:

Mr. Thwaites contended, somewhat faintly, that, as
[Mr. Adams] has a brother of the full blood and as there was evidence that the
chance of a full brother having the same nine DNA bands is one in 220, this
weakened the DNA evidence against [Mr. Adams].  But, as there was no evidence
as to the brother’s actual DNA profile nor any suggestion that he might have
committed the offence, the point leads nowhere and we disregard it.

[
587
]

In

McLeod
, at para.
31
, the Court concluded as follows:

In short, while there appears to be some foundation
of theory or principle underpinning this leg of Mr. McLeod’s submission, it is
of no consequence in the absence of at least some evidence giving it practical
shape and form.  Because there is no such evidence, his argument amounts to a
suggestion the trial judge should have speculated about the possibility of a
blood relative being involved in the crime.  The judge made no error in declining
to do that.

[
588
]

Similarly,
in the present case, while there is some foundation for the proposition that
Mr. Belbin’s DNA could be transferred from the ground to the pyjama top under
certain conditions, that proposition is of no consequence in the absence of at
least some evidence giving it “practical shape and form” – that is, some
evidence that Mr. Belbin deposited his DNA in the backyard of 72 Ch. by
spitting or urinating there.  As there is no evidentiary basis upon which to
draw this inference, the Court ought not to speculate about the possibility of
such an event having occurred.

[
589
]

I
would note that even if the court were to infer that Mr. Belbin spat or
urinated somewhere in the backyard of a house with which he had no connection,
his DNA could not have been transferred from the ground to the pyjama top unless
E.L.’s assailant coincidentally happened to place her on the ground in exactly
the same spot upon which Mr. Belbin left his DNA.

[
590
]

Counsel
for Mr. Belbin relied on the Court of Appeal decision in
R. v. Wills
,

2014 ONCA 178
, and the “fingerprint cases” of
R. v. Mars
(2006),
2006 CanLII 3460 (ON CA)
, 205
C.C.C. (3d) 376 and
R. v. D.D.T
.,
2009 ONCA 918
, in support of her
position that the DNA evidence in this case is insufficient on which to ground
a conviction.

[
591
]

In

Mars
, the appellant was charged with robbery.  The only issue at trial
was identity.  The evidence connecting the appellant to the robbery was his
fingerprint found on a pizza box that was used as part of a ruse to gain entry
into the apartment.  The appellant was arrested four months after the robbery.
There was no way of identifying when the appellant’s fingerprint was placed on
the box.  The appellant was convicted at trial.

[
592
]

In
allowing Mars’ appeal, the court held that the fingerprint evidence, standing alone,
did not permit any inference as to when the appellant’s fingerprint was placed
on the box.  There was also no evidence from which it could be inferred that
the appellant touched the pizza box in connection with the robbery.  That being
the case, the failure of the appellant to offer any other explanation by way of
testimony or through some other evidence was of no consequence.  His failure to
testify or otherwise advance an “innocent” explanation could not add weight to
the Crown’s case so as to justify drawing what would otherwise be an
unreasonable inference of guilt.

[
593
]

In
my view,
Mars
is clearly distinguishable from the case at bar.  In
Mars
,
there was no evidence as to when the fingerprint was placed on the pizza box.
In the present case, the timing of the transfer of Mr. Belbin’s DNA to E.L.’s
pyjama top is clear.  The transfer took place in that narrow window of time
between the point when E.L. was taken from her bed and when the perpetrator
fled from the backyard.  The question of how Mr. Belbin’s DNA was transferred
to the pyjama top is in issue but the circumstances in which a direct or
indirect transfer could have occurred are limited.  There was either a transfer
of Mr. Belbin’s DNA to the pyjama top as a result of his having had direct
contact with it during the time frame referred to above, or an indirect
transfer of his DNA from the ground to the pyjama top as a result of E.L.
having been placed on the ground where Mr. Belbin’s DNA was present.  The
expert testimony was to the effect that a lot of factors would have to line up
in a certain way for that particular indirect transfer to occur but, more
importantly, as stated previously, there is no evidentiary basis to infer that Mr.
Belbin’s DNA was on the ground in that location in the first place.

[
594
]

In

Wills
, the appellant was convicted of robbery and other offences
connected to a home invasion.  It was alleged that the appellant and another
male, while masked, forced themselves into a home, assaulted the two occupants,
and fled with a small amount of cash.  Identity was the main issue.  Neither victim
could identify their assailants.  However, DNA evidence linked the appellant to
two bandanas used by one or both perpetrators, and a baton similar to the
weapon used to beat the male victim was seized from the appellant’s residence
two months after the robbery.  The appellant was convicted.

[
595
]

In
dismissing the appeal, the Court in
Wills
held that while the DNA
evidence suggested some connection between the appellant and the robbery, and
went some way toward identifying the appellant as one of the perpetrators, it
was not sufficient alone.  However, when the DNA evidence was combined with the
baton found in the appellant’s residence, there was evidence that could
establish that the appellant was one of the robbers.

[
596
]

In

Wills
, the police located the white bandana that one of the victims had
pulled from the face of the first robber.  The second bandana was found in the
ravine along the escape route followed by the robbers.  It was a fair inference
that both bandanas were worn during the robbery by either or both robbers.
Wills’ DNA profile was found on both bandanas.  However, the Crown expert could
not say when the DNA was placed on the bandanas or estimate how long it may
have been on them.  Nor could the expert say how the DNA had come to be placed
on the bandanas.  It could have been as a result of direct or indirect contact.

[
597
]

In
holding that the DNA evidence alone could not support the inference that the
appellant was one of the perpetrators or that either bandana belonged to the
appellant, the Court, at para. 36, stated:

The expert evidence called by the Crown precluded
those inferences based exclusively on the DNA evidence.  Like the fingerprint
evidence in
R. v. Mars
(2006),
2006 CanLII 3460 (ON CA)
, 205 C.C.C. (3d) 376, at paras.
20-21

(Ont. C.A.) and
R. v. D.D.T
.,
2009 ONCA 918
, at para.
26
, the DNA
evidence alone could not say when the DNA was placed on the bandanas and
therefore could not identify the appellant as the perpetrator of the robbery.
There had to be other evidence which, combined with the DNA evidence, would
permit a finding that the appellant was the perpetrator, e.g, see
R. v.
Samuels
,
2009 ONCA 719
; and
R. v. Wong
,
2011 ONCA 815
.

[
598
]

The
present case may be distinguished from
Wills
in the same way that it is
distinguishable from
Mars
.  In
Wills
, there was no evidence as to
when the DNA was placed on the bandana, which, like a pizza box, is an object
that can be passed around from person to person.  The circumstances in the
present case are very different since, as already stated, there is no issue as
to when Mr. Belbin’s DNA was deposited on the pyjama top.  The issue is
restricted to the question of how it came to be there – namely, as a result of
a direct transfer from Mr. Belbin himself or an indirect transfer as a result
of his having spat or urinated on the ground where Esther was placed by her
assailant.

[
599
]

Given
that there is no evidentiary basis on which to infer that Mr. Belbin spat or
urinated in the backyard of D[…]2, the only reasonable inference in all of the
circumstances is that his DNA was placed on the pyjama top as a result of a
direct transfer – that is, by Mr. Belbin having had direct contact with the top.
Based on Mr. Currie’s testimony, such a transfer is consistent with Mr. Belbin having
touched the pyjama top while removing it from E.L. and tossing it aside.

[
600
]

Mr.
Currie could not say what type of body fluid was the source of Mr. Belbin’s DNA
on the pyjama top.  In the circumstances of this case, that fact does not
diminish the strength or power of the DNA evidence in identifying Mr. Belbin as
the perpetrator.  Mr. Belbin’s DNA profile was the only profile detected on the
pyjama top that did not belong to E.L. or a male family relative.  The presence
of S.L.’s DNA is of no significance as he had bathed E.L. that night, dressed
her in the pyjamas, and put her to bed.  Mr. Belbin was a complete stranger to
E.L. and had no connection whatsoever with the residents at D[…]1.

[
601
]

I
also find the fact that Mr. Belbin’s DNA was found on a piece of E.L.’s
clothing, as opposed to on her body, is not significant in the circumstances of
this case.  There is an extremely close link between E.L.’s body and the pyjama
top as she was wearing it when she was abducted and up until the time that her
assailant removed it.

[
602
]

In
the circumstances of this case, I am satisfied that the DNA evidence, in and of
itself, proves beyond a reasonable doubt that it was Mr. Belbin who entered D[…]1
in the early hours of the morning on December 26, 2011, abducted the sleeping
five-year-old complainant from her bed, and committed the offences of sexual
assault and touching for a sexual purpose.  However, there is other evidence
that supports this finding, namely, the perpetrator’s direction of flight.

[
603
]

I
have found that not too much weight can be placed on S.L.’s description of the
perpetrator.  However, his testimony that the perpetrator fled in an easterly
direction and struggled to get over something on the eastern portion of the
property line is reliable.  The direction of flight is significant as it allows
for the inference that the perpetrator was the same person R.G. observed a
short time later.

[
604
]

R.G.
heard a scream, waited a minute or so, and then went outside.  He saw a male emerge
from between two houses east of his own house, jog past his house, and
disappear between two houses west of his house.  The backyard of one of those
houses backs onto the backyard of D[…]3, where Mr. Belbin lived.  For the
reasons already stated, I found R.G.’s description of the male’s approximate
age, size, stature and the way that he moved to be reliable.  His description
of the male as about 19 years old, 5 feet 10 inches tall, weighing about 180
pounds and with a good build – “healthy” and “strong” are consistent with Mr.
Belbin’s appearance.

[
605
]

The
flight route described by S.L., together with the evidence of R.G., is consistent
with Mr. Belbin trying to make his way back home after committing these
offences.  The police presence was such that he could not walk back to his
house along D[…] without being detected.  It makes sense that he would follow the
semi-circle route described by R.G., which would have led him into the backyard
of 81 A. Street, from where he could access his own backyard and his apartment.

[
606
]

In
order to convict on the basis of circumstantial evidence, the trier of fact
must be convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that the guilt of the accused is
the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the proven facts.  I am so
convinced in this case.  Having considered all of the evidence and submissions
of counsel, I am satisfied that the Crown has met its burden.  The presence of
Mr. Belbin’s DNA on E.L.’s pyjama top, and S.L.’s and R.G.’s evidence of a
direction of flight by the perpetrator that led to Mr. Belbin’s home, establish
beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Belbin committed these offences.

CONCLUSION

[
607
]

For
